record.title: SimLife-BP tests long-horizon behavioral-rule inference in synthetic household simulations
record.summary: Peng et al. present SimLife-BP, a benchmark for inferring symbolic behavioral patterns from long synthetic household timelines. The current v2 paper describes 106 episodes, up to 48.23 hours and 120 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs; tasks test direct, counterfactual, noisy-counterfactual and inverse reasoning under three hint levels. Across reported model evaluations, performance depends strongly on the evidence pipeline: most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average question accuracy, while Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with full hints over noiseless text-only evidence. The authors also report shortcutting by frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when patterns change. These are paper-reported results in scripted Sims 4 simulations with deterministic symbolic rules and generated dialogue, not evidence of real human understanding or deployed household-agent performance.

claims.text: The current v2 paper describes 106 synthetic episodes up to 48.23 hours/120 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs and four reasoning question types at three hint levels.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s full-hint noiseless text-only condition, Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy; most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average accuracy.

evidence_gaps.description: The benchmark results, generated episodes and input pipelines have not been independently audited or reproduced.
Transfer from deterministic synthetic household rules and generated dialogue to independently observed human behavior is unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If reproduced and extended beyond synthetic households, the benchmark would materially change how long-context agents are evaluated for personalization, memory and adaptation by testing rule inference across extended multimodal evidence rather than recall alone. The present study uses scripted deterministic rules and synthetic dialogue, and its large input-pipeline effects prevent broad claims about human understanding; its current importance is notable for evaluation design, not demonstrated real-world capability.
limitations: All results are paper-reported; no independent execution or reproduction was performed.
The benchmark uses synthetic Sims 4 activity and deterministic symbolic rules; it does not establish inference about real people or actual household-agent performance.
Dialogue is generated using model-assisted pipelines and spot-checked; its validity as natural human evidence remains uncertain.

Vision-plus-language evaluation uses a two-stage video-to-diary then text-QA pipeline, while noiseless text-only input exposes structured evidence; performance differences therefore mix perception, summarization and reasoning.
Hint levels provide varying prior rule information; full-hint/noiseless conditions do not represent the ordinary deployed-agent setting.
Transfer to independently collected behavior, other simulators and real-world long-term interaction is unmeasured.
brief.summary: Peng et al. present SimLife-BP, a benchmark for inferring symbolic behavioral patterns from long synthetic household timelines. The current v2 paper describes 106 episodes, up to 48.23 hours and 120 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs; tasks test direct, counterfactual, noisy-counterfactual and inverse reasoning under three hint levels. Across reported model evaluations, performance depends strongly on the evidence pipeline: most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average question accuracy, while Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with full hints over noiseless text-only evidence. The authors also report shortcutting by frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when patterns change. These are paper-reported results in scripted Sims 4 simulations with deterministic symbolic rules and generated dialogue, not evidence of real human understanding or deployed household-agent performance.

technical.claimed_result: The authors argue that models may predict frequent outcomes without recovering the underlying rule, and that performance improves when relevant evidence is cleaner and structured. Their v2 paper reports these patterns within its scripted, deterministic synthetic environment; external validity is unestablished.
technical.compute_or_cost: The appendix reports evaluation can take several hours to seven days per model using vLLM 0.19.0 on one to four NVIDIA A40 GPUs; total benchmark-generation and end-to-end inference costs were not reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v2 paper describes 106 episodes up to 48.23 hours/120 in-game days and 1,439 questions, organized into 381 tasks per hint level. It reports that most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average accuracy; under full hints, Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with noiseless text-only evidence (L-N). Authors report frequent reliance on simple frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when behavioral patterns change. These results are author-reported benchmark measurements.
technical.implementation_status: The authors provide a project website and describe a simulation/data-generation and evaluation pipeline. the research desk inspected the primary paper but did not execute the benchmark code or independently validate the generated episodes.
technical.mechanism: SimLife simulates multi-character household activity in The Sims 4 with visual observations, game-action logs and generated dialogue. SimLife-BP builds long video chains from days whose actions satisfy explicit temporal or event-based if-then rules, then asks four binary question types—direct prediction, counterfactual, noisy counterfactual and inverse reasoning—at three rule-hint levels. The visual baseline first summarizes video windows into diaries and then answers from concatenated text; text-only baselines receive cleaner structured inputs.
technical.novelty: Combines extended simulated household timelines, multimodal contextual cues, explicit underlying behavioral rules, four complementary reasoning queries and dynamic pattern changes in a benchmark designed to distinguish surface prediction from rule inference.
technical.regime: Synthetic household activity built on The Sims 4. Episodes use scripted deterministic symbolic rules with temporal or event-based conditions; video and generated dialogue are aligned with simulator action logs. Tasks contain four binary question types and three hint levels. The vision pipeline summarizes windows before text-only QA; the noiseless language-only condition provides structured oracle-filtered evidence.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes episode construction, rule formalization, question design and input pipelines. The public artifacts and model runs have not been independently executed; simulation and generated-dialogue validity and transfer to independently collected human behavior remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the paper, modality and evidence-pipeline comparisons include vision-plus-language diary summaries, language-only responses over noisier action-log text (L), and language-only responses over noiseless structured text (L-N), with full, partial and no-hint conditions. The comparison reveals input/evidence effects but does not isolate a general reasoning mechanism independent of those pipelines.

brief.title: SimLife-BP tests long-horizon behavioral-rule inference in synthetic household simulations
brief.why_it_matters: The benchmark separates long-context storage from the harder task of inferring and revising a behavioral rule when evidence is distributed across time and modalities. Its large reported gap between raw video-plus-language and structured noiseless text shows that evaluation can be dominated by evidence extraction and organization before rule reasoning is measured. The synthetic deterministic rules and staged diary-summary pipeline make the result useful for evaluation design but limit claims about people or real-world assistants.
